bull.b: The record backlog provides meaningful visibility into future rental revenue and reduces reliance on securing entirely new demand each quarter. With $635 million of annualized rent scheduled to commence in H2 2026, contracted growth should support operating momentum over the next several quarters.

Strong renewal spreads indicate that existing data center capacity retains pricing power as contracts reset, supporting durable same-site revenue and NOI growth. This ability to reprice occupied infrastructure can sustain returns without requiring equivalent portfolio expansion or customer additions.

The cable landing station broadens Digital Realty’s connectivity ecosystem by linking subsea infrastructure with terrestrial networks, cloud platforms and colocation. That integration can deepen customer embeddedness, improve the usefulness of the Los Angeles campus, and create durable interconnection demand when operational.

bear.b: Higher development spending increases near-term funding needs and places greater importance on asset recycling and private capital to preserve financial flexibility. Large capital requirements can also delay free-cash-flow conversion, making growth more dependent on disciplined execution and continued access to financing.

Reliance on large, episodic hyperscale leases can make commencements, occupancy growth and revenue timing uneven even when underlying demand remains strong. Customer concentration in this segment raises execution sensitivity because a delayed or shifted project may affect several quarters of growth.

Stricter local approval, clean-energy and water requirements can lengthen permitting timelines or raise development costs in affected markets. Because Digital Realty is expanding its data-center footprint, broader community scrutiny could constrain the pace and economics of future capacity delivery.
